# Analysis

## Hypothesis 1: More Popular Repositories Exhibit Higher Development Activity
The central question in this study investigates whether more popular repositories also exhibit higher development activity.
Popularity is approximates by the number of GitHub stars per repository, while activity is measured by the average number of
pull requests merged per week. The underlying hypothesis is that more popular repositories attract more contributors and therefore
should show higher pull requests throughput.`

To obtain the activity metric, the OrientDB function `averageWeeklyMergedPRs` is applied to each repository. This function counts all
merged pull requests belonging to a repository and determines the time span between the first and last merged pull requests. These
two values are then combined to derive an average merge rate per week. This computation is performed for every repository, combined
with its star count, and then visualized as a scatter plot, once with linear axes and once with logarithmic scaling on both axes.

![Popularity vs Activity](img/popularity_vs_activity.png){#fig-popularity_vs_activity fig-align="center"}

A visual inspection of @fig-popularity_vs_activity shows that the initial hypothesis is not supported by the data. The points
are scattered across the plot without any clear upward or downward pattern, and repositories with very different star counts often have
similar levels of activity. Most repositories between 100000 and 500000 stars cluster around 0.5 and 10 merged pull requests per week.
In summary, the plot provides no clear evidence that higher popularity is associated with higher activity.

## Hypothesis 2: Programming Language Influences Development Activity
The second hypothesis examines whether the primary programming language of a repository is associated with its development activity.
As before, activity is measured by the average number of pull requests per week. The hypothesis is that repositories with different
languages exhibit different development activity.

To test this hypothesis, the analysis first computes the activity metric for each repository and then groups repositories by their primary
language. For each language, it calculates the average activity and visualizes the resulting values as a horizontal bar chart sorted
by activity.

![Average merged pull requests per week per language](img/language_vs_activity.png){#fig-language_vs_activity fig-align="center"}

The @fig-language_vs_activity shows clear differences in average activity between languages, which supports the hypothesis that the
primary language is associated with development activity. Languages such as C++, TypeScript, Rust, and Python lie towards the upper
end of the distribution with relatively high activity. In contrast, languages like Markdown, HTML, CSS, and Dockerfile appear in the
lower end with substantially lower activity.

Two qualitative observations may help to interpret the differences. First, general purpose programming languages tend to be associated
with higher activity, which is plausible given that they often back actively maintained software projects. Second, many highly starred
repositories whose primary language is a markup or configuration language turn out, upon manual inspection, to be collection-style or
resource-oriented projects rather than conventional code bases. Examples include 'awesome' which is a list of interesting topics or
collections of free public APIs.
These explanations remain speculative, but the plot provides clear evidence in support of the original hypothesis that repositories
using different primary languages exhibit different levels of development activity.
